common_name: Sweet Lorane Fava Bean (Cover Crop Fava)

planting.note: Sow in fall for overwintering in mild-winter regions, or as early as the ground can be worked in spring farther north; Sweet Lorane tolerates cold into the low 20s F once established.

directions: Inoculate large seed with pea/vetch-type rhizobia and sow 1.5-2 inches deep in a firm seedbed, either in fall for overwintering where winters stay above the low 20s F, or as early as possible in spring elsewhere. Sweet Lorane is a small-seeded, open-pollinated fava selected specifically for cover-crop and green-manure use rather than table use, producing dense, leafy stands and a heavy root system that scavenges nitrogen and breaks up compacted ground. It flowers earlier and more heavily than large-seeded table favas, drawing in bumblebees and other early-season pollinators. Terminate by cutting or crimping at early-to-mid bloom, when nitrogen fixation peaks, and let the succulent stems break down for two to three weeks before following with a heavy-feeding crop.

common_name: Indianhead Black Lentil (Cover Crop / Green Manure Lentil)

planting.note: Sow as early as the soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer in mild climates for a short-season fall cover; a tolerant, quick-fixing lentil bred for biomass rather than seed yield.

directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed shallowly, about 1 inch deep, into a firm seedbed; Indianhead is a black-seeded lentil selection developed in Canada specifically for green-manure and companion cover-crop use rather than culinary lentil production, valued for its vigorous early growth and reliable nitrogen fixation on the Northern Plains. Its short, sprawling habit makes it a good companion in mixes with taller cereals like oats or barley, which give the vining stems something to lean on. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or light tillage at flowering to capture the most fixed nitrogen before the crop sets pods. It tolerates cool soils and light frost better than most warm-season legumes, making it a useful early-spring or short-window fall cover.

common_name: Alice White Clover (Large-Leaved Grazing and Cover Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast in spring or late summer onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; Alice establishes into a persistent, spreading perennial stand suited to pasture, orchard understory, or living mulch.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at a light rate onto a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/4 inch deep. Alice is a large-leaved white clover bred in New Zealand for vigorous stolon spread and strong regrowth after grazing or mowing, giving it more bulk and ground coverage than common Dutch white clover while remaining lower-growing than giant ladino types. Its aggressive stoloniferous habit lets it fill bare patches quickly, making it a reliable nitrogen-fixing living mulch between perennial crop rows or a component in long-term pasture and cover mixes. Mow periodically to prevent taller companion plants from shading it out, and expect the stand to persist and spread for several years once established.
sources: University of Kentucky College of Agriculture

common_name: Freedom Red Clover (Root-Rot-Resistant Cover Crop Clover)

planting.note: Sow in late summer 6-10 weeks before first fall frost, or frost-seed in late winter; Freedom was bred for extended stand life under wet, disease-prone conditions.

directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed onto a firm, prepared seedbed and rake to a shallow quarter-inch depth. Freedom is a USDA-released red clover bred for improved resistance to northern and southern anthracnose and root rot, giving it a longer productive stand life than many older red clover types on the wetter or more disease-prone soils where standard red clover thins out after a single season. It fixes substantial nitrogen and produces heavy biomass for a single planting, supporting one or two cuttings before it is terminated. Mow or till under at early bloom for the greatest nitrogen release to a following crop, and expect a second flush of regrowth if only partially cut.

planting.note: Sow from early spring through summer; Nitro is a fast, Peruvian-type annual alfalfa bred to be terminated the same season rather than grown as a persistent perennial forage stand.

directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/2 inch deep. Nitro is a Peruvian-type annual alfalfa selected specifically for rapid, single-season green-manure use rather than the multi-year persistence of standard perennial alfalfa hay types, producing a tall, fast-growing stand and abundant nitrogen-rich biomass within about two to three months. Because it lacks strong winter hardiness compared to perennial cultivars, it winterkills reliably in cold climates, simplifying termination without herbicide or tillage. Mow or till under at bud-to-early-bloom stage for the greatest nitrogen contribution, and expect a vigorous regrowth flush if only partially cut before final incorporation.
